author: Melville
title: Ishmael and Ahab
about: Ishmael tells the story of a whaling voyage on the Pequod of Nantucket, whose captain, Ahab, has lost a leg to a white sperm whale, Moby Dick, and makes the crew swear to hunt it. In the first passage, from the opening paragraph, Ishmael says why he goes to sea. The second gives the opening and the close of Ahab’s speech alone in his cabin on the evening of the oath. In the third, near the end, another captain asks Ahab’s help to find a lost boat.

view.says: For Auden this is a tragedy of possibility: it could have gone otherwise. Ahab starts where a Greek hero finishes, in great misfortune, which tempts him and gives him a choice. He chooses wrongly and goes on doing so. Only his last refusal, of the Rachel’s plea for help, makes his end necessary. In defiance, Ahab says that fate acts and not he.
view.quote: The defiant man and the obedient man use the same words “It is not I but Fate,” but their meaning is opposite.
view.source: “The Christian Tragic Hero,” *The New York Times Book Review*, 16 December 1945, pp. 1 and 21; *The Enchafèd Flood* (1950; Vintage Books edition, 1967), pp. 136–37 and 140 (the quotation is on p. 137)

lenses.label: Sentence
lenses.caption: The first sentence here has 87 words. Four clauses headed by whenever come first, each longer than the last. Then comes the main clause, which could stand alone: I account it high time. Kept to the end, it holds the sense open. Auden wrote that Ishmael goes to sea to escape spleen and his own lack of power, and has consciousness and no will. In the first and third clauses Ishmael says I find myself, a phrase for what one does without meaning to. In the fourth his low spirits get the upper hand of me, and it takes a principle to prevent me. The main verb, account, means consider.
lenses.why: The main clause waits behind four whenever clauses; in two Ishmael finds himself doing things, in the fourth his low spirits and a principle act on him; the main verb means consider; Auden’s Ishmael has consciousness and no will.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, with a count of the words in each clause. What a main clause kept to the end does: Wikipedia, under Periodic sentence. The senses of *find oneself* and *account*: Wiktionary and Merriam-Webster. Auden on Ishmael: *The Enchafèd Flood*, p. 112, and “The Christian Tragic Hero” (1945).

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: anaphora
lenses.plain: the same word at the head of clause after clause
lenses.caption: All four clauses are headed by the same word, whenever (the fourth after and especially). A word repeated at the head of clause after clause is anaphora, and it makes the clauses one list. The list runs from his face to his soul, to coffins and funerals, to people’s hats in the street, and one then answers all four. Auden prints part of this sentence beside Coleridge and Baudelaire as a description of how it feels to be a solitary who cannot go the crowd’s way. Whenever means every time that, so each item is one that comes back; the sentence before calls going to sea a way I have.
lenses.why: Four clauses are headed by whenever, which means every time that, so the sentence lists states that keep coming back; Auden prints part of it as a description of how it feels to be a solitary.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. Anaphora as *Silva Rhetoricae*, Merriam-Webster and the *Encyclopaedia Britannica* define it, and *whenever* as Merriam-Webster does. The words *a way I have* are in the sentence before, in [Chapter 1](#/read/moby-dick/c001:0). Auden prints part of the sentence in *The Enchafèd Flood*, p. 35, in an argument that runs from p. 34 to p. 36.

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: From the Latin *voluntas*, will, with *in-*, not.
Short for *hypochondria*, and in use from about 1710 for depression of the spirits.
From the Latin *deliberare*, to weigh well; *libra* is a pair of scales.
From the Greek *methodos*, at first a following after; *hodos* is a way or road.
The next sentence sets his going to sea beside Cato, who threw himself on his sword.

lenses.caption: Hypos is short for hypochondria and meant low spirits, fits of melancholy. Involuntarily is built on the Latin word for will, with in-, meaning not; it goes with what Ishmael does, at coffin warehouses and funerals. Deliberately comes from the Latin for weighing well, as on scales, and methodically from a Greek word for a following after, built on the word for a road. These two, the words of purpose and method, go only with the acts a principle must prevent: stepping into the street, knocking off hats. Auden’s image for the condition this sentence describes is Dürer’s Melancholia, who knows how to build her city and lacks the will.
lenses.why: Involuntarily, at root not willed, goes with what Ishmael does; deliberately and methodically go only with acts a principle must prevent; Auden’s image of the condition is a figure who knows how and lacks the will.
lenses.stands: The history of the words: Online Etymology Dictionary, under *hypo*, *involuntary*, *voluntary*, *deliberate* and *method*; Merriam-Webster and Wiktionary, under *hypo*. Which adverb goes with which act can be seen in the passage. Auden on Dürer’s *Melancholia*: *The Enchafèd Flood*, p. 36.

lenses.meterName: the foot of blank verse: an off-beat, then a beat

points.say: Four feet to the first stop, then five, six, one and two. Only the second phrase has the five feet of a line of blank verse.
A poet’s contraction of *wherever*. It saves a syllable, and the beat stays even.
Two stresses, then a stop. Two more fall together, on *fixed* and the first syllable of *purpose*. They slow the voice, and here it leaves the rule.
The last sentence starts on a stress, against the rule, and ends in step with it.

lenses.caption: Ahab speaks alone, in prose, under a stage direction. The rule under the words repeats the foot of blank verse, the verse of Shakespeare’s plays: an off-beat, then a beat. The voice follows it through the first paragraph’s eighteen feet, with a light stress off the beat at pale and a foot, let them, that can be heard turned round. From is laid to I rush it follows twenty more, with one foot turned at Over and one beat left unstressed in unerringly. Chapter 16 says a whaleman of great force learns a lofty language and is formed for noble tragedies. For Auden, Ahab dies unrepenting, like Shakespeare’s tragic heroes.
lenses.why: Ahab’s prose keeps the rising beat of blank verse in a chapter set as a play; Chapter 16 says a whaleman of great force learns a lofty language; Auden wrote that Ahab dies unrepenting, like Shakespeare’s tragic heroes.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, the opening and close of [Chapter 37](#/read/moby-dick/c037:0). Blank verse and its foot as the *Encyclopaedia Britannica* and Merriam-Webster define them, and *where’er* as Wiktionary does; stresses that fall together slow a line, according to Paull F. Baum, *The Principles of English Versification*, chapter 5. The narrator on the whaleman’s language: [Chapter 16](#/read/moby-dick/c016:42). Auden on Ahab and Shakespeare’s heroes: “The Christian Tragic Hero” (1945).

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: metaphor
lenses.plain: one thing spoken of as another
lenses.caption: Ahab has dared the gods to swerve him. His answer is a picture: the path to his purpose is laid with iron rails, and his soul is grooved to run on them. Speaking of one thing as another is a metaphor. At the start he says I for the ship, which leaves a wake, a track the waves swell to cover; at the end his way is iron. Neither verb, is laid or is grooved, names a doer. Earlier the verbs are his: I’ve willed, I’ll do. Auden quotes this sentence where he says that defiance and obedience both say it is fate, not I, and mean opposite things.
lenses.why: Ahab answers his dare with a railroad, iron where the speech began with a wake, in verbs that name no one who laid the rails; Auden quotes the sentence for the defiant man saying it is fate, not he.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. Metaphor as *Silva Rhetoricae* and Merriam-Webster define it; *whelm* as the Online Etymology Dictionary gives it. The dare to the gods and the verbs *I’ve willed* and *I’ll do* come earlier in the speech, in [Chapter 37](#/read/moby-dick/c037:4). Auden quotes the sentence in *The Enchafèd Flood*, p. 137.

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: From the Latin *turbidus*, muddy, full of confusion; *turba* is turmoil, a crowd.
From the Latin *invidere*, to look at with malice; an obsolete English sense is malignant or spiteful.
To cover completely by the 1550s, to engulf like a flood by the 1660s: the second half of *overwhelm*.
To *groove*, to cut a channel in, dates from the 1680s; from 1842 a *groove* was also a fixed routine, a rut.
To *sound* is to measure the depth of water with a line and lead.
To *rifle* is to plunder, from the fourteenth century; from the 1630s it is also to cut spiral grooves in a gun barrel.
*Un-*, not, with *err*, from the Latin *errare*, to wander or go astray.

lenses.caption: Envious comes from the Latin for looking with malice, and once meant spiteful. In the chapter before, Ahab says he sees inscrutable malice in the whale; here he gives the waves a word of ill will. The surgeon of another ship, the Samuel Enderby, later calls the whale’s malice mere awkwardness, and Auden notes that Ahab cannot bear such sanity. The waves swell to whelm his track, to cover it completely. Rifled means plundered, and since the 1630s also cut with grooves, as a gun barrel is; grooved is his word for his own soul. Unerringly is built on err, from the Latin for wandering: it means making no mistake, not going astray.
lenses.why: Ahab’s word for the waves once meant spiteful, and malice is what he sees in the whale; unerringly and grooved say he does not stray; Auden notes that he cannot bear the surgeon’s sanity.
lenses.stands: The history of the words: Online Etymology Dictionary, under *envious*, *envy*, *whelm*, *rifle*, *groove*, *err* and *unerring*; Wiktionary, under *envious*, for the old sense spiteful. Ahab on the whale’s malice: [Chapter 36](#/read/moby-dick/c036:39). The surgeon: [Chapter 100](#/read/moby-dick/c100:35). Auden on Ahab and the surgeon: *The Enchafèd Flood*, p. 137.

facts.after: Chapter 41 opens with the narrator naming himself as one of that crew.
facts.ranks: Starbuck is chief mate, Stubb second mate and Flask third. Flask has no solo speech.
facts.epilogue: The Epilogue begins by saying that the drama is done.
facts.audenQuotes: Auden quotes from each of the three solo speeches: Ahab’s vow and the iron-rails sentence from Chapter 37 (The Enchafèd Flood, p. 137), Starbuck from Chapter 38 (p. 124) and Stubb from Chapter 39 (pp. 126–27).
facts.otherRuns: Chapters 119 to 122 are the other run of chapters with stage directions, four in a row.

lenses.caption: Twelve of the 135 chapters carry stage directions; five stand in a row, this one second. Chapter 36 gathers all hands on the quarter-deck toward evening. Then three men speak alone, each farther forward and later: Ahab in the stern cabin at sunset, the chief mate at the mainmast at dusk, the second mate up the foremast in the first night watch. Last, at midnight on the forecastle, come 25 of the crew, each speech headed with its speaker. From Chapter 37 to Chapter 40 the narrator says nothing. Auden wrote that the crew give themselves away in their words and acts, while Ishmael and the reader only record.
lenses.why: Chapter 37 is second of five in a row that carry stage directions, moving from stern to bow, the last four with no narrator; Auden says the crew give themselves away in words and acts while Ishmael only records.
lenses.stands: A count, in the text printed here, of the chapters that set a stage direction on a line of its own; asides in brackets inside a paragraph are not counted. The places, hours and speakers are those of [Chapters 36](#/read/moby-dick/c036:0) to [40](#/read/moby-dick/c040:0). Where each place is on a ship: Merriam-Webster. Auden: *The Enchafèd Flood*, pp. 112 and 119.

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: antimetabole
lenses.plain: the same words said again in the opposite order
lenses.caption: Captain Gardiner, whose boy is lost in a boat, says he will not go until Ahab agrees, and asks him to do as he would be done by. That is the Golden Rule of the Gospels. Ahab’s reply has the two verbs in the opposite order: he will not do it, and he must go. Words repeated in the opposite order are called antimetabole, or more loosely chiasmus, a crossing; this one runs from one speaker to the other. With go Ahab puts must where Gardiner had will, and Gardiner had already told him you must. For Auden, Ahab’s end becomes necessary only with the answer he gives here.
lenses.why: Ahab’s refusal has the other captain’s verbs in crossed order, will not go and do becoming will not do and must go; for Auden this refusal is the point after which Ahab’s end is necessary.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. The Golden Rule is Matthew 7:12 and Luke 6:31; antimetabole and chiasmus are as *Silva Rhetoricae* defines them. The lost boy and Gardiner’s *you must* come earlier in [Chapter 128](#/read/moby-dick/c128:9). Auden on the refusal: “The Christian Tragic Hero” (1945).

lenses.label: Sentence
lenses.caption: Each of Gardiner’s two sentences here has a clause hung on it. He will not go till Ahab says yes. Ahab is to do as he would be done by in the like case: he too has a boy. The narrator says Ahab’s voice moulded every word of the answer. Its four sentences here are short, and none has such a clause. The last joins a blessing, a wish and a statement with and and but, and ends I must go. The next paragraph calls the refusal unconditional. Auden says that in refusing Gardiner, Ahab counterfeits the Gospel text that a disciple must hate father, mother, wife and children.
lenses.why: Gardiner’s plea carries clauses with till and as, the like case of a father; Ahab’s four short sentences carry none, and the narrator calls his refusal unconditional; Auden says it counterfeits the Gospel text on hating father and children.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. That Ahab too has a boy is Gardiner’s next sentence, in [Chapter 128](#/read/moby-dick/c128:14); the word *unconditional* is the narrator’s, in the [paragraph after the answer](#/read/moby-dick/c128:16). Auden on the refusal as a counterfeit of the Gospel text: *The Enchafèd Flood*, p. 140. The text is Luke 14:26.

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: A sailor’s word since the 1680s, probably from the Dutch *houd vast*, hold fast.
A contraction of *God be with ye*, written *godbwye* in the 1570s and shaped by *good day* and *good evening*.
Jeremiah 31:15, where the King James Bible spells her name *Rahel*; Matthew 2:18 quotes the verse for the children Herod has killed.
The closing words of Jeremiah 31:15 in the King James Bible. A modern version has: *because they are no more*.

lenses.caption: Avast is a ship’s order to stop, and good-bye is a contraction of God be with ye. Ahab says it twice, then God bless ye. His next wish has no God in it: may I forgive myself. In his paragraph on Ahab, Auden writes of a religious hero whose god is his own will, set in defiance. The chapter’s last sentence takes its words from Jeremiah, where Rachel weeps for her children and refuses comfort because they were not. Matthew quotes that verse for the children Herod killed. For Auden the Rachel stands for people caught up in the mystery of existence who neither understood nor chose it, as those children were in Christ’s birth.
lenses.why: Ahab asks God’s blessing for Gardiner and forgiveness of himself; Auden writes of a hero whose god is his own will; the last sentence gives the ship Jeremiah’s words for Rachel, and Auden compares the ship to Herod’s innocents.
lenses.stands: The history of *avast* and *good-bye*: Online Etymology Dictionary. What Ahab wishes can be seen in the passage. Rachel’s verse is Jeremiah 31:15, quoted in Matthew 2:16–18 (King James Version). Auden: *The Enchafèd Flood*, pp. 138 and 140, on the hero whose god is his own will, and p. 61, on the Rachel.

facts.sameWords: Ahab’s question is given in his own words in six chapters (52, 71, 100, 115, 128, 131); in Chapter 100 he hails the Samuel Enderby twice. In the last four of these chapters it is the same five words. In Chapter 81 he questions the Jungfrau’s captain and his words are not given; in Chapter 91 Stubb asks for him; in Chapter 54 no question is given.
facts.asked: Two ships ask something of Ahab. The Jungfrau wants lamp oil and is supplied (Chapter 81). The Rachel wants help in her search and is refused (Chapter 128). The Bachelor’s captain invites him aboard, which asks nothing of him (Chapter 115).
facts.after: The chase follows in Chapters 133 to 135. In the Epilogue the Rachel, still searching for *her missing children*, picks up Ishmael.

lenses.caption: The Pequod meets nine ships, and the Rachel is the eighth. At six of the meetings Ahab’s question about the White Whale is given in his own words, at the last four in the same five. The answers differ: a trumpet lost overboard, a story kept from him, a warning, two ships that know nothing, a captain who lost an arm, a disbeliever, a lost boat, a burial. Auden reads the nine as so many ways of standing toward the mystery of existence. Two of the ships ask something of Ahab: the Jungfrau gets her lamp oil, and the Rachel is refused. In the Epilogue the Rachel picks up Ishmael.
lenses.why: The Rachel is the eighth of the nine ships the Pequod meets, and the one whose plea for help Ahab refuses; Auden reads the nine as types of how people stand to the mystery of existence.
lenses.stands: The nine meetings as the text printed here tells them, in Chapters [52](#/read/moby-dick/c052:2), [54](#/read/moby-dick/c054:2), [71](#/read/moby-dick/c071:12), [81](#/read/moby-dick/c081:5), [91](#/read/moby-dick/c091:13), [100](#/read/moby-dick/c100:1), [115](#/read/moby-dick/c115:7), [128](#/read/moby-dick/c128:2) and [131](#/read/moby-dick/c131:2). The rescue is in the [Epilogue](#/read/moby-dick/epilogue:2). Auden on the nine ships: *The Enchafèd Flood*, pp. 60–61.

auden.says: Auden takes Melville’s own word, *isolato*, for Ishmael’s kind: a man who keeps to a land of his own. He sets part of the sentence shown in the first passage beside lines of Coleridge’s “Dejection” and Baudelaire’s “Spleen,” as reports of how it feels to be a solitary who cannot go the way of the crowd. In a city where tradition no longer walls anyone in, he says, no direction is closed to Ishmael and nothing in him makes any one direction necessary, so he has to do something drastic and goes to sea.
auden.source: *The Enchafèd Flood* (1950; Vintage Books edition, 1967), pp. 34–36

auden.says: Auden’s essay of 1945 calls the book four things at once: an epic, a tragedy and a quest, each heroic, and a religious quest told as allegory. It is also, he adds, an American novel of its century. The essay ends with Ishmael. He is no character, Auden says, since a character is someone who wills and acts, and Ishmael has consciousness without will: he knows and does nothing. Not having started to live, he cannot die, and the book leaves him an orphan who has yet to make his first choice. Ahab, unrepenting like Shakespeare’s tragic heroes, goes to a death that was not necessary and that he chose.
auden.source: “The Christian Tragic Hero,” *The New York Times Book Review*, 16 December 1945, pp. 1 and 21

auden.says: Auden reads the nine ships the Pequod meets as so many kinds of people and societies, each standing differently toward the mystery of existence: the old, who may have known it and cannot pass it on; those who know and do not tell; those who make an idol of it or have lost their wits to it; the lazy and the greedy, who will never notice it; those who meet it with plain sense and endurance; the lucky and light-minded, who say there is none; those caught up in it who neither understood nor chose it; and those it has left grieving.
auden.source: *The Enchafèd Flood* (1950; Vintage Books edition, 1967), pp. 60–61

auden.says: On the page where he comes to the Rachel, Auden writes that Ahab is glad of pain, the typhoon for one, and takes a calm, happy day for a temptation. He calls this a false copy of the way saints accept suffering and mistrust pleasure.
auden.quote: His whole life, in fact, is one of taking up defiantly a cross he is not required to take up.
auden.source: *The Enchafèd Flood* (1950; Vintage Books edition, 1967), p. 140

auden.says: In class in the fall of 1941 Auden named Ahab and the White Whale, or Kafka’s K. and the Castle, as examples of how a single person stands to his fate, which was the subject of the course, and then played the second movement of Beethoven’s Fourth Piano Concerto. A student wrote down what he asked the class to hear: the piano sets itself against the orchestra, its fate, and strikes out alone; before long it has lost its way; it steadies only when it takes the orchestra back. He asked whether that return is in time.
auden.source: Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan,” in *W. H. Auden: The Far Interior*, edited by Alan Bold (1985), pp. 135–36

auden.says: A student who shared Auden’s house remembered him saying many times that the book is really a poem of the epic kind, and that this is how to read it. In a note to *New Year Letter*, published in 1941, Auden called American writing the writing of solitary people and said that most American books could open the way this one does, with *Call me Ishmael*. Melville’s sea and whale, he wrote there, are no more real than a drawing-room in Henry James; he called most American novels parables.
auden.source: Charles H. Miller, *Auden: An American Friendship* (1983), p. 135; W. H. Auden, *New Year Letter* (1941), note to line 1566, pp. 152–53

caveats: Auden’s 1945 essay “The Christian Tragic Hero,” his note in *New Year Letter* and Charles Miller’s memoir were read here only in extracts from scanned copies, not from end to end. His words in class are known from Donald Pearce, a student who wrote them down after the class.

The second passage is prose, and its marks show one way of saying it: *pale*, *let them*, *Swerve me*, *through* and the last syllable of *unerringly* can fairly be stressed otherwise, and *envious* can be said as two syllables or three.

The crossing of *go* and *do* in the third passage runs from one speaker to the other, with other sentences between; the handbooks define antimetabole and chiasmus within one sentence or in clauses that follow each other.

The count of twelve chapters with stage directions takes only directions set on a line of their own: asides in brackets inside a paragraph are not counted, nor is the title of Chapter 29, which is worded as a stage direction.

Auden’s sentence about a hero whose god is his own will begins with *if* and is said of the religious hero in general. It stands in his paragraph on Ahab, and the page sets it beside Ahab’s wish to forgive himself.
